Topic: Red Wine Quality Prediction using Supervised Classification & Random Forest Pipeline

Wine Quality Prediction Using Machine Learning & Random Forest

1. Problem Statement & Motivation

Sensory wine certification conducted by human expert sommeliers is inherently subjective, prone to sensory fatigue, and resource-intensive. In global wine commercialization, wineries require reliable, automated, and reproducible methods to predict whether a fermented wine batch will meet commercial "Good / Export Quality" standards based on standard analytical chemistry.

This project formulates wine quality classification as a supervised learning problem. Using 11 physicochemical laboratory measurements (acidity, sugars, sulfur dioxide, density, pH, sulphates, and alcohol), we model the relationship between laboratory parameters and sensory ratings. The primary objective is to evaluate three contrasting machine learning paradigms—Logistic Regression (linear baseline), Support Vector Machine (SVM with RBF Kernel) (kernel margin classifier), and Random Forest (non-linear ensemble)—to discover the optimal predictive pipeline while rigorously avoiding data leakage.

2. Dataset Description

The dataset is the authoritative Portuguese "Vinho Verde" red wine dataset from the UCI Machine Learning Repository (Cortez et al., 2009). It comprises 1,599 raw observations characterized by 11 continuous physicochemical features and 1 sensory quality rating (discrete scale from 3 to 8).

3. Data Preprocessing & Leakage Prevention

Rigorous preprocessing was conducted in the following order:

  1. Missing Value Audit: Verified 0 missing/NaN entries across all 12 columns.
  2. Duplicate Elimination: Detected 240 identical feature records. In laboratory wine testing, identical measurements represent either repeated logging or identical vat samples. Dropping duplicates prevented identical records from appearing in both train and test partitions, yielding 1,359 unique observations.
  3. Target Binarization: Binarized into Class 1 (Good Quality, Score ≥ 6) and Class 0 (Normal/Low Quality, Score < 6), establishing a balanced distribution (719 Good vs 640 Normal/Low).
  4. Stratified Train-Test Split (80/20): Partitioned into 1,087 training samples and 272 testing samples using stratify=y and random_state=42.
  5. Pipeline Encapsulation: StandardScaler was encapsulated inside a scikit-learn Pipeline alongside the classifiers. The scaling parameters (mean and standard deviation) were fitted exclusively on training folds during cross-validation, strictly preventing test distribution leakage.
Figure 2: Pearson correlation matrix across physicochemical attributes and quality target. Note strong positive correlation with alcohol (+0.48) and strong negative correlation with volatile acidity (-0.39).

4. Algorithm Selection and Rationale

Three complementary machine learning algorithms were selected to compare distinct mathematical paradigms:

  • Logistic Regression (Linear Baseline): Parametric linear model optimizing log-odds. Selected to establish whether wine quality classes are linearly separable in standardized feature space.
  • Support Vector Machine (SVM with RBF Kernel): Non-linear maximum-margin classifier mapped into infinite-dimensional Hilbert space. Calibrated via Platt scaling (CalibratedClassifierCV) to yield well-calibrated posterior probabilities.
  • Random Forest Classifier (Ensemble Architecture): Non-parametric ensemble of 200 decorrelated decision trees with randomized feature splits. Selected because enological quality involves complex non-linear feature interactions (e.g., high alcohol buffering high volatile acidity) which tree splits natively capture.

5. Training, 5-Fold Cross-Validation & Test Evaluation

Model selection was governed strictly by 5-Fold Stratified Cross-Validation on the training set (N=1,087), not by optimizing on the test score. After establishing the winning architecture via CV, the final models were evaluated on the completely unseen test set (N=272).

6. Receiver Operating Characteristic & Feature Attribution

The ROC curves illustrate the trade-off between True Positive Rate (Sensitivity) and False Positive Rate (1 - Specificity) across all decision thresholds. Random Forest achieved the highest ROC-AUC of 0.8363, outperforming SVM (0.8238) and Logistic Regression (0.8116).

Figure 5: Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve comparison. Random Forest demonstrates superior discriminative power across all operational thresholds.
Figure 6: Random Forest Gini feature importance ranking. Alcohol (15.5%), sulphates (12.3%), and volatile acidity (11.8%) constitute the dominant chemical determinants of wine quality.

7. In-Depth Analysis & Discussion

7.1 Which Model Won and Why?

The Random Forest Classifier won across both 5-Fold Cross-Validation (75.44%) and Out-of-Sample Test Accuracy (79.04%), with an F1-Score of 0.7986 and ROC-AUC of 0.8363. The primary reason is that sensory wine quality is governed by non-linear thresholds: moderate acidity enhances quality only when balanced by sufficient alcohol; similarly, volatile acidity exhibits a sharp threshold above which acetic vinegar spoilage dominates. Decision tree ensembles naturally segment these multidimensional non-linear regions, while bootstrap aggregation reduces individual tree variance.

7.2 What the Errors Mean in Industrial Practice

In commercial enology, classification errors carry asymmetric economic consequences:

  • False Positive (Type I Error): The model labels a subpar wine batch as "Good Quality". Bottling flawed wine under a premium label causes severe commercial harm—damaging winery reputation, triggering retailer returns, and risking legal disputes.
  • False Negative (Type II Error): The model labels an export-worthy batch as "Normal/Low Quality". The winery diverts premium wine into discounted bulk blending. This represents an opportunity cost in foregone margin, but does not harm brand prestige or consumer trust.

7.3 Which Metric Matters Most?

Because false positives cause brand degradation, Precision (81.29%) is the primary operational metric for premium reserve bottling. However, from an overall enological management perspective, ROC-AUC (0.8363) is the most critical metric because it proves the model provides smooth, calibrated probabilities, allowing cellar masters to tune the decision threshold (e.g., raising it from 0.50 to 0.70 to achieve 95% precision for flagship vintages).

7.4 Limitations

  1. Absence of Phenolic Data: The dataset omits anthocyanins, tannins, and Total Polyphenol Index (TPI), which govern mouthfeel astringency and color stability.
  2. Regional Specificity: The dataset reflects the cool-climate Portuguese Vinho Verde region and may require recalibration for warm-climate varietals.

8. Mapping to Course Outcome (CO5)

Course Outcome: "CO5 – Solve real life problems using appropriate machine learning models and evaluate the performance measures."

This investigation fully satisfies and operationalizes CO5:

  1. Real-Life Problem Formulation: Addressed objective quality screening in commercial viticulture, converting sensory wine grading into an actionable binary classification framework.
  2. Appropriate Machine Learning Models: Implemented and compared three diverse architectures (Logistic Regression, Support Vector Machine, and Random Forest) using scikit-learn Pipelines with standardized scaling.
  3. Rigorous Performance Evaluation: Evaluated models across comprehensive dimensions—5-Fold Stratified Cross-Validation, Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-Score, Confusion Matrices, ROC-AUC curves, and Gini feature importance.
  4. Deployment & Real-World Applicability: Delivered a serialized model via joblib and an interactive Streamlit application enabling real-time laboratory quality predictions and enological diagnostics.
